paragraphs.text: The appellants allege that they are threatened by Mexican society as a whole due to their sexual orientation. They also claim to have been threatened with death on several occasions by a man named XXXX, a drug dealer who wanted to sell his products to customers at XXXX XXXX where Mr. XXXX worked in Mérida (state of Yucatan).

In their memorandum, the appellants contest the RPD's conclusions regarding the first prong of the IFA, which represents the sole determinative issue on appeal. They argue that they cannot safely relocate to any of the proposed cities because they will be persecuted by reason of their sexual orientation everywhere in the country.

The appellants submitted new evidence in support of their refugee protection claim when perfecting their appeal record in February 2020: * A-1: Three news articles dated October and November 2019 reporting discrimination, particularly against those whose sexual orientation is not heterosexual.

The appellants then submitted nine additional documents as new evidence, dated October 1, 2020: * A-2: A letter from XXXX XXXX XXXX dated August 29, 2020; * A-3: A newspaper article titled [translation] "Javier Found, Young Man Missing From CDMX Burned in Cuernavaca," dated August 25, 2020; * A-4: A newspaper article titled [translation] "Javier Burned, Wrapped in LGBT+ Flag, Found in Cuernavaca," dated August 25, 2020; * A-5: Article from the Human Rights Commission in Mexico City, dated July 2, 2020; * A-6: A newspaper article titled [translation] "Organizations Reveal Tlaxcala Without Instructions to Eradicate Sexual Orientation Discrimination," dated May 17, 2020; * A-7: A newspaper article titled [translation] "Faced With an Epidemic, Demands for Guaranteed Rights for the LGBT Community," dated May 20, 2020; * A-8: A newspaper article titled [translation] "Call to Address Discrimination Against the LGBT Community in Work Centres," dated June 27, 2020; * A-9: A newspaper article titled [translation] "Hateful Homicide because of LGBT Phobia in Mexico," dated May 2, 2020; * A-10: A newspaper article titled [translation] "Homophobic Hate Crimes in Mexico Without Official Statistics," dated May 2, 2020.

Here, the appellants identified an agent of persecution, namely XXXX, and identified a risk due to the country's insecurity and the homophobic behaviour of Mexican society as a whole. XXXXability to act and interest

In their testimony, both appellants stated that although XXXXwent after them, his behaviour had more to do with the fact that he was banned from selling drugs than it did with their sexual orientation. The RPD nonetheless sought to find out why the latter would attempt to track them down in the three proposed cities. They stated that he was seeking vengeance. When asked to identify what methods XXXXmight use to locate them, the appellants stated that he certainly had the means, but did not have the knowledge.

In their memorandum, the appellants state that the RPD erred because its reasoning in this regard was tainted by a significant error, that is, the fact that this conclusion [translation] "replaces objective evidence with hypothetical deductions."11

According to the appellants, Mexican society is such that they will be persecuted due to their sexual orientation no matter where they attempt to relocate. They testified at the hearing and report in their memorandum that they have faced several situations of discrimination in their lives, including situations involving employment and housing, that they have been intimidated and insulted because of their sexual orientation, and that they have been physically assaulted.12

The appellants submitted Exhibit A-6, a newspaper article from a local Mexican media outlet dated May 17, 2020, titled "Organizations Reveal Tlaxcala Without Instructions to Eradicate Sexual Orientation Discrimination." According to the appellants, this article demonstrates that discrimination has not yet been [translation] "eradicated," nor has persecution on the basis of sexual orientation, notably because same-sex marriage is not permitted, hate-motivated killings are not punishable and conversion therapies are not prohibited.

The appellants submitted Exhibit A-7, an article from a local Mexican newspaper dated May 20, 2020, titled "Faced With an Epidemic, Demands for Guaranteed Rights for the LGBT Community." According to the appellants, this article demonstrates that discrimination and persecution on the basis of sexual orientation still occur in the state of Hidalgo, where Pachuca is located. Members of the LGBT community are allegedly denied their right to access health care and this violation has been exacerbated under the COVID-19 pandemic. Hate crimes against members of this community reportedly go unpunished.

The appellants also submitted exhibits A-2 to A-4, which involve the murder of an LGBT activist in Mexico City, Exhibit A-5, a report from the Human Rights Commission in Mexico City, and Exhibit A-10, a newspaper article that addresses the problems associated with compiling hate crimes against the LGBT community in Mexico City.

According to the appellants, these exhibits call into question the safe nature of Mexico City. More specifically, the appellants argue that they demonstrate the absence of [translation] "areas open to homosexual individuals" (paragraph 41 of the RPD's decision), that hate crimes are current (paragraph 42 of the RPD's decision), and that they are not properly accounted for, consequently undermining the RPD's conclusion that few people with diverse sexual orientation, gender identity or expression are murdered (paragraph 51 of the RPD's decision).
The appellants did not challenge the RPD's conclusions regarding this second prong of the IFA, save for a brief mention relating to their profile.18
